topic: The President and the executive branch

notes.front: What is the executive branch?
notes.back: The branch that enforces federal laws; the President is in charge of it.
notes.explanation: It is the second of the three branches, distinct from the lawmaking Congress taught in the last topic.
notes.example: Like a school's staff, who carry out the rules the school board writes.

notes.front: Who is the President?
notes.back: The head of the executive branch; elected for four years and can be elected only twice.
notes.explanation: Every other term in this topic describes the President's powers, limits or team.
notes.example: Like a town's mayor, elected by the people and limited to two terms in the role.

notes.front: What does the 22nd Amendment say?
notes.back: “No person shall be elected to the office of the President more than twice”; added 1951.
notes.explanation: It is the constitutional source of the two-term limit just mentioned.
notes.example: Example: Franklin Roosevelt was elected four times. After that, the 22nd Amendment (1951) set a limit of two.

notes.front: What does the Vice President do?
notes.back: Works for the President; is President of the Senate; becomes President if the President can no longer serve.
notes.explanation: The Vice President's Senate role and succession role both matter for later cards.
notes.example: Example: if the President dies, the Vice President becomes President.

notes.front: What is the line of succession?
notes.back: The order of who becomes President: President, then Vice President, then Speaker of the House.
notes.explanation: It fixes who takes over, and in what order, if the President cannot serve.
notes.example: Like a school's named backup plan: the deputy head takes over first, then the senior teacher.

notes.front: What does it mean for the President to “sign a bill”?
notes.back: When the President agrees with a bill passed by both houses, the President signs it into law.
notes.explanation: Signing is what turns a passed bill into an actual law.
notes.example: Like a town's final approval that turns a council-approved plan into an actual rule.

notes.front: What is a veto?
notes.back: The President refuses to sign a bill; it does not become law unless Congress overrides the veto.
notes.explanation: It is the President's main check on Congress's lawmaking power.
notes.source: Study guide p.22; Ben's Guide (two-thirds override)
notes.example: Congress can still make it law if two-thirds of the House and two-thirds of the Senate vote yes.

notes.front: What does “Commander in Chief” mean?
notes.back: The President is in charge of everyone serving in the U.S. military (Armed Forces).
notes.explanation: It is one of the President's named constitutional powers, separate from Congress's power to declare war.
notes.source: Study guide p.26; Constitution Art. II, sec. 2
notes.example: Like the one person who has final authority over a town's entire fire and police service.

notes.front: What is meant by the President as “chief diplomat”?
notes.back: USCIS's own accepted answer: one power of the President, representing the United States in other countries.
notes.explanation: It is one of six listed accepted answers to “name one power of the president.”
notes.example: Like the one person a school authorises to speak for it to other schools.

notes.front: What is a federal judge?
notes.back: A judge on the Supreme Court or a lower federal court; nominated by the President and approved by the Senate.
notes.explanation: Naming judges is one of the President's powers, but the Senate must also approve the choice.
notes.example: Like a school naming a new head teacher that the school board must still approve before they start.

notes.front: What is the Cabinet?
notes.back: A group of advisors; the President's Cabinet advises the President.
notes.explanation: It is one of the executive branch's named parts, made up of the Cabinet-level positions taught next.
notes.example: Like a head teacher's own team of senior staff who give advice.

notes.front: What are Cabinet-level positions?
notes.back: The leaders of the executive departments (mostly called Secretaries) plus other officials the President chooses; USCIS lists 22.
notes.explanation: Each of the 22 listed positions has its own card later in this topic, as a complete set.
notes.example: Like the named head of each department in a school, such as maths or sport.

notes.front: What is the Attorney General?
notes.back: The leader of the Department of Justice; unlike most Cabinet-level officials, not called a Secretary.
notes.explanation: It is one named exception to the “Secretary” naming pattern most Cabinet-level positions follow.
notes.example: Like a school's head of discipline, whose title is not "teacher" even though the job is similar.

notes.front: What are executive departments and agencies?
notes.back: Parts of the executive branch that help the President enforce laws, protect the country and serve the people.
notes.explanation: They are the working parts of the executive branch beyond the President personally.
notes.example: Like a school's different teams, each carrying out one part of running the school.

notes.front: What is the Electoral College?
notes.back: The process that elects the President; a compromise between election by Congress and election by popular vote.
notes.explanation: It is the actual mechanism by which the President is chosen, rather than a direct nationwide vote.
notes.source: NARA, About the Electoral College; M-1778 Q49
notes.example: Each state has electors. The electors choose the President.

notes.front: What is a political party, in this context?
notes.back: An organisation that nominates candidates; the two major US parties are the Democratic Party and the Republican Party.
notes.explanation: Presidents and most members of Congress run for office as a party's nominee.
notes.example: Example: in a presidential election, the Democratic Party picks one person and the Republican Party picks another.

notes.front: The President of the United States is elected for how many years?
notes.explanation: A President is elected every four years, for example in 2024 and 2028. One of the 20 questions for 65/20 applicants. (65/20)

notes.front: The President of the United States can serve only two terms. Why?
notes.explanation: USCIS also accepts the plain reason the amendment exists. Other accepted answers: To keep the president from becoming too powerful.

notes.front: What is the name of the President of the United States now?
notes.explanation: One of the 20 questions for 65/20 applicants; check uscis.gov/citizenship/testupdates before an interview. (65/20) Other accepted answers: Donald Trump; Trump.

notes.front: If the president can no longer serve, who becomes president?
notes.back: The Vice President (of the United States).
notes.explanation: This is the first step of the line of succession.

notes.front: Name one power of the president?
notes.explanation: USCIS lists six accepted answers; each has its own primer earlier in this topic. Other accepted answers: Vetoes bills; Enforces laws; Commander in Chief (of the military); Chief diplomat; Appoints federal judges.

notes.front: Who is Commander in Chief of the U.S. military?
notes.explanation: Only this one accepted answer is listed.

notes.front: Who signs bills to become laws?
notes.explanation: Only this one accepted answer is listed.

notes.front: Who vetoes bills?
notes.explanation: Only the President can veto (say no to) a bill. One of the 20 questions for 65/20 applicants. (65/20)

notes.front: Who appoints federal judges?
notes.explanation: The Senate must still approve the President's choice, as the primer explains.

notes.front: The executive branch has many parts. Name one?
notes.explanation: USCIS also accepts the Cabinet or the federal departments and agencies. Other accepted answers: Cabinet; Federal departments and agencies.

notes.front: What does the President's Cabinet do?
notes.back: Advises the President (of the United States).
notes.explanation: This is the Cabinet's only listed accepted answer.

notes.front: What are two Cabinet-level positions?
notes.back: Attorney General and Secretary of State.
notes.explanation: USCIS lists 22 accepted positions; each has its own card next, since this is a complete set. Other accepted answers: Secretary of Agriculture; Secretary of Commerce; Secretary of Education; Secretary of Energy; Secretary of Health and Human Services; Secretary of Homeland Security; Secretary of Housing and Urban Development; Secretary of the Interior; Secretary of Labor; Secretary of Transportation; Secretary of the Treasury; Secretary of Veterans Affairs; Secretary of War (Defense); Vice-President; Administrator of the Environmental Protection Agency; Administrator of the Small Business Administration; Director of the Central Intelligence Agency; Director of the Office of Management and Budget; Director of National Intelligence; United States Trade Representative.

notes.front: Why is the Electoral College important?
notes.back: It decides who is elected president.
notes.explanation: USCIS also accepts describing it as a compromise between popular election and congressional selection. Other accepted answers: It provides a compromise between the popular election of the president and congressional selection.

notes.front: In what year was the 22nd Amendment, limiting Presidents to two terms, added?
notes.explanation: It came after Franklin Roosevelt's four elected terms, taught in a later topic.

notes.front: Which branch of government is the President in charge of?
notes.explanation: The President heads it, distinct from Congress, which makes the laws it enforces.

notes.front: Who is the head of the US executive branch, elected for a four-year term?
notes.explanation: This office is the subject of nearly every other card in this topic.

notes.front: A President has already been elected twice. Can they be elected a third time?
notes.back: No: the 22nd Amendment limits a President to two elected terms.
notes.explanation: This constitutional limit, not custom, is what stops a third term.

notes.front: Who is President of the Senate and next in line if the President cannot serve?
notes.explanation: Both roles belong to the same office at once.

notes.front: If both the President and Vice President cannot serve, who is next?
notes.explanation: The line of succession moves through these offices in a fixed order.

notes.front: Both houses of Congress pass a bill and the President agrees with it. What does the President do?
notes.explanation: Signing is what completes a bill's path into law.

notes.front: The President disagrees with a passed bill and refuses to sign it. What is this called?
notes.explanation: A veto blocks the bill unless Congress overrides it.

notes.front: Who has final authority over everyone serving in the US Armed Forces?
notes.back: The President, as Commander in Chief.
notes.explanation: This is one of the President's named constitutional powers.

notes.front: Who nominates federal judges, subject to Senate approval?
notes.explanation: Nominating is the President's power; confirming is the Senate's.

notes.front: Who gives the President advice as a formal group of senior officials?
notes.explanation: Its members are the Cabinet-level positions taught as a set.

notes.front: What is the general name for the 22 leadership roles USCIS lists, such as Secretary of State?
notes.explanation: Most, but not all, of these positions are called “Secretary.”

notes.front: Beyond the President personally, what carries out the executive branch's day-to-day work?
notes.explanation: They do the ongoing work of enforcing laws and serving the public.

notes.front: The President is not chosen by a single nationwide popular vote. What process chooses them instead?
notes.explanation: It is a deliberate compromise between popular and congressional election.

notes.front: What is the difference between signing a bill and vetoing a bill?
notes.back: Signing: the President agrees, and the bill becomes law. Vetoing: the President refuses, and it fails unless Congress overrides it.
notes.explanation: They are the two opposite things a President can do with the same passed bill.
notes.contrast: Both question 43 and question 44 test the same fact from opposite directions: who signs, and who vetoes.
